title: The Siege of Alesia
summary: Caesar shuts eighty thousand Gauls inside eleven miles of works, then turns fourteen more outward against the army that marches to relieve them. A hidden column of sixty thousand nearly breaks his north camp before his own cavalry takes it in the rear.

units.label: Legions on the lines in the plain
The north camp under Mont Réa
Legions on the Montagne de Bussy
Legions on the Montagne de Flavigny

phases.label: The relief army camps on the outer hill
phases.caption: Six weeks after Caesar sat down before the town the relief army comes over the hills from the south-west and camps a mile outside the Roman lines. Behind those lines the siege is already finished work: eleven miles of contravallation with twenty-three redoubts, fourteen of circumvallation facing outward, and between them the legions in four sectors. Antonius and Trebonius hold the plain, the north camp lies under Mont Réa, Labienus is on Bussy, and the last camps stand on Flavigny. Vercingetorix sent his cavalry away by night before the works closed; the Mandubii were turned out of the town and died between the walls. Eighty thousand men wait inside on corn that ran out days ago.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. Caesar gives the arrival no time word (VII.79), and an afternoon arrival is a reading that leaves the next morning for the deployment. Of the twelve phases only three carry a time Caesar states, noon on day 1, midnight opening day 3 and noon on day 4, and the other nine say so in their own notes.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting (Nap III.10.XI-XIII) laid on his planche 25, georeferenced on the villages it draws. Those are Seigny, Grignon, Ménétreux-le-Pitois and Alise-Sainte-Reine on the west sheet, and Bussy-le-Grand, Darcey, Flavigny-sur-Ozerain, Gissey-sous-Flavigny and Hauteroche on the east, checked against SRTM 1 arc-second. The 1991-97 Franco-German excavations confirm the works in the plain and the camps on the heights and reject Napoleon's camp D at the foot of Mont Réa. Caesar's north camp is real, on the north-west hill, and nobody has located it, so camp D stands in for it here and on the map. Every later phase uses the same siting.

The battle opens on the relief army's arrival rather than on the investment because no source counts the days between them. They are more than thirty and fewer than about fifty, and putting a day number on it would assert a count nobody has. The six weeks are the caption's work instead.

Dates: six strings and not one of them a calendar date, because no source dates the battle. September is the convention and is uncited wherever it is given. Livius puts the surrender on 30 August in Julian terms, Brunaux on 27 September, and Ramsey and Raaflaub argue for the relief army about 7 November and the capitulation about 13 November Julian, with the civil calendar running some twenty-five days ahead of the sun. The 20 September 52 BC that sorts this battle in the library is a sorting convention and not a claim about the day. The five entries after the first are day numbers alone, which is what the caption band's clock column has room for at desktop width, where it neither wraps a date nor clips one.

Numbers: Caesar's eighty thousand besieged (VII.71), eight thousand horse and two hundred and forty thousand foot outside (VII.76). Plutarch has three hundred thousand outside and a hundred and seventy thousand in the town (27.2). Modern estimates run to a fifth of Caesar's. Caesar never totals his own army.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXIX, opening sentence
references.quote: In the meantime, Commius and the rest of the leaders, to whom the supreme command had been intrusted, came with all their forces to Alesia, and having occupied the entire hill, encamp not more than a mile from our fortifications.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXIX, the works
references.quote: The circuit of that fortification, which was commenced by the Romans, comprised eleven miles.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXI, the cavalry sent away
references.quote: he silently dismisses the cavalry in the second watch, [on that side] where our works were not completed

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXVIII, the Mandubii
references.quote: The Mandubii, who had admitted them into the town, are compelled to go forth with their wives and children.

references.locator: book XL, chapter 40, section 4, the fate of the Mandubii
references.quote: Now these perished most miserably between the city and the camp, because neither party would receive them.

phases.label: The relief horse fills the plain; the besieged come out before the town
phases.caption: In the morning the relief army leads its cavalry out and fills the whole three miles of plain, with the foot posted a little back on the higher ground. From the town, which commands the plain end to end, the besieged see them: there is shouting across the works, and Vercingetorix brings his army out of the camp to stand before the town, filling the nearest trench with hurdles and earth against the moment for a sally. Caesar mans both faces of the lines, so that every cohort knows its own post.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. Caesar has only 'The following day' (VII.79) and fixes nothing until noon, so a morning deployment is a reading.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

The besieged turn from facing the inner line at 90 to facing the plain at 270 between this phase and the last, the one exact half-turn in the battle. It resolves clockwise, through the north, over the hill they are standing on. Their position is the west slope below the town, which is where Napoleon puts the camp they drew out to.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXIX, the plain filled
references.quote: The following day, having led forth their cavalry from the camp, they fill all that plain, which, we have related, extended three miles in length, and draw out their infantry a little from that place, and post them on the higher ground.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXIX, the town's view
references.quote: The town Alesia commanded a view of the whole plain. The besieged run together when these auxiliaries were seen; mutual congratulations ensue, and the minds of all are elated with joy.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXIX, the sally prepared
references.quote: Accordingly, drawing out their troops, they encamp before the town, and cover the nearest trench with hurdles and fill it up with earth, and make ready for a sally and every casualty.

phases.label: The cavalry battle in the plain opens
phases.caption: At noon Caesar orders his cavalry out of camp to open the action. The Gauls have scattered archers and light foot among their horse, and men on the Roman side go down to them unexpectedly and leave the fight. The legions stand on the works and watch, and so does the whole of both Gallic armies, the one shut inside the ring and the one outside it, shouting to their own men from every quarter. Nothing done in that plain can be hidden from anybody.
phases.notes:
Time: Caesar's own. 'After fighting from noon almost to sunset' (VII.80) fixes the opening at 12:00, one of the three times here that are not estimates.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1. The cavalry action is drawn in the plain between the lines and the relief camp, which is where Caesar puts it. No source gives a point in it.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXX, the cavalry sent out
references.quote: orders the cavalry to issue forth from the camp and commence action

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXX, the archers among the horse
references.quote: The Gauls had scattered archers and light-armed infantry here and there, among their cavalry, to give relief to their retreating troops, and sustain the impetuosity of our cavalry.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXX, the watching armies
references.quote: both those who were hemmed in by the line of circumvallation and those who had come to aid them, supported the spirits of their men by shouts and yells from every quarter.

references.locator: book VII, chapter 80, the length of the fight
references.quote: The fight lasted, and the victory was doubtful, from noon almost to sunset

phases.label: The Germans charge; the Gallic horse flees to camp
phases.caption: Towards sunset the Germans mass and charge home in one body, and the Gallic horse breaks. The archers left standing in the plain are surrounded and cut to pieces, and along the rest of the field the Roman horse rides the fugitives back to their own camp and gives them no chance to rally. Those who had come out of Alesia to watch go back into the town dejected. The next day the relief army spends making hurdles, ladders and grappling hooks; this picture holds through it.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. Caesar's 'almost to sunset' is the only mark, and sunset at 47.54 N in late September falls about 18:00, computed here rather than taken from any source. This phase then holds thirty hours, through the quiet day Caesar calls 'the interval of a day' (VII.81), so it plays at the fastest rate in the battle.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

Strength: the relief horse drops to 80%, a reading of a rout in which the archers among them were 'surrounded and cut to pieces' and the horse were ridden back to camp. Caesar gives no number for it, or for any other loss in this battle except the seventy-four standards.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXX, the German charge
references.quote: the Germans, on one side, made a charge against the enemy in a compact body, and drove them back; and, when they were put to flight, the archers were surrounded and cut to pieces.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXX, the pursuit and the return to the town
references.quote: But those who had come forth from Alesia returned into the town dejected and almost despairing of success.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXI, the quiet day
references.quote: The Gauls, after the interval of a day, and after making, during that time, an immense number of hurdles, scaling ladders, and iron hooks

phases.label: Midnight: the relief storms the plain works and Vercingetorix sallies
phases.caption: At midnight the relief army goes out of camp without a sound and comes up against the works in the plain, then raises a shout so that the town will know it. They throw down hurdles and sweep the rampart with slings, arrows and stones. Vercingetorix hears the shout, sounds the trumpet and leads his men out of the town at the inner line. Every Roman is at the post he was given days before; the darkness hides everything, and the wounds fall on both sides. Antonius and Trebonius strip the far redoubts of men and send them wherever the pressure tells.
phases.notes:
Time: Caesar's own. 'silently went forth from the camp at midnight' (VII.81) is the second of the three stated times. Midnight is written as day 3 at 00:00 rather than day 2 at 23:59 because the assault and its repulse both fall after it.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

State: the besieged stay intact. They came out, they filled the nearest trenches, and they never reached the works (VII.82), so the arrow says what they meant and the state says what happened. The two detachment arrows are the drafts Caesar names from the more distant redoubts; he gives no number for them. Dio adds the concealed pits, which Caesar describes at VII.73 and does not mention again here.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXI, the midnight approach
references.quote: silently went forth from the camp at midnight and approached the fortifications in the plain

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXI, the assault
references.quote: they began to cast down hurdles and dislodge our men from the rampart by slings, arrows, and stones

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXI, Vercingetorix leads his men out
references.quote: Vercingetorix having heard the shout, gives the signal to his troops by a trumpet, and leads them forth from the town.

references.locator: book VII, chapter 81, section 1, the time word
references.quote: media nocte silentio ex castris egressi ad campestres munitiones accedunt

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXI, the drafts from the far redoubts
references.quote: But Marcus Antonius, and Caius Trebonius, the lieutenants, to whom the defence of these parts had been allotted, draughted troops from the redoubts which were more remote

references.locator: book XL, chapter 40, section 5, the concealed pits
references.quote: the Romans had dug secret pits in the places which were passable for horses and had fixed stakes in them

phases.label: Day comes; the Gauls draw off, the besieged too late
phases.caption: At a distance the Gauls did execution by weight of missiles; close in they empale themselves on the spurs or are shot down by the engines on the towers. As day comes on, afraid of a sally out of the higher camp against their open flank, they draw off to their own army. The besieged, still bringing up the gear Vercingetorix had prepared and filling the nearest trenches, learn that their countrymen have gone before they ever reach the works, and go back into the town having done nothing. That day the Gallic leaders take counsel and send out scouts.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. Caesar has 'when day drew nigh' (VII.82), and sunrise at this latitude in late September falls about 06:00, computed rather than sourced. This phase holds twenty-four hours, through the council of VII.83 and the choosing of the sixty thousand.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1. The higher camp whose sally they feared reads as Flavigny, on the attackers' right hand, which is Napoleon's reading.

Strength: the relief foot drops to 90% on Caesar's 'many wounds on all sides' and his later 'twice repulsed with great loss'. There is no number.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXII, the spurs and the mural darts
references.quote: after they came nearer, they either unawares empaled themselves on the spurs, or were pierced by the mural darts from the ramparts and towers, and thus perished

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXII, the withdrawal
references.quote: After receiving many wounds on all sides, and having forced no part of the works, when day drew nigh, fearing lest they should be surrounded by a sally made from the higher camp on the exposed flank, they retreated to their countrymen.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXII, the besieged too late
references.quote: they learned the retreat of their countrymen before they drew nigh to the fortifications. Thus they returned to the town without accomplishing their object.

phases.label: Before dawn: Vercassivellaunus hides behind Mont Réa
phases.caption: The scouts have found the one weak place: a hill on the north side that the circuit could not take in, where two legions under Reginus and Rebilus hold a camp on ground that slopes against them. Sixty thousand men are picked out of the whole army from the states with the best name for courage, and given to Vercassivellaunus the Arvernian, Vercingetorix's own kinsman. He marched at the first watch, was nearly round before dawn, and now lies hidden behind the mountain resting his men. The attack is to go in when it seems to be noon. The track drawn from the relief camp to Mont Réa is the plate's straight line and not the road: Napoleon III takes the march round west of the Brenne by the heights of Grignon and Fain, a night's sweep the map has no second phase to bend it through.
phases.notes:
Time: Caesar's words rather than a clock: 'having issued from the camp at the first watch, and having almost completed his march a little before the dawn' (VII.83). The 05:30 is an estimate hung on that.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

Track: Napoleon routes the night march round by the heights of Grignon and Fain, a wide sweep west of the Brenne. The plate draws the straight line between this phase and the last, which runs across the plain and over the Roman works. It is not the road, and a phase in between would have nothing to say. Caesar's 'on the north side' is north-west seen from the town, which is Mont Réa.

Absence: the sixty thousand are listed among the units from the start and drawn only from here, because they are picked out of the relief army on day 3 and do not exist as a body before that. A phase is allowed to leave a unit out, and theirs are one unbroken run of phases. The six before this one say nothing about them at all.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIII, the hill and the camp
references.quote: There was, on the north side, a hill, which our men could not include in their works, on account of the extent of the circuit, and had necessarily made their camp in ground almost disadvantageous, and pretty steep.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIII, the sixty thousand chosen
references.quote: select from the entire army sixty thousand men; belonging to those states which bear the highest character for courage

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIII, the night march
references.quote: He, having issued from the camp at the first watch, and having almost completed his march a little before the dawn, hid himself behind the mountain, and ordered his soldiers to refresh themselves after their labour during the night.

references.locator: book VII, chapter 83, section 7, the watches the march is measured in
references.quote: Ille ex castris prima vigilia egressus prope confecto sub lucem itinere post montem se occultavit

phases.label: Noon: the north camp, the plain and the town attacked at once
phases.caption: As noon draws on, all three attacks go in together. Vercassivellaunus comes down off Mont Réa on the north camp; the relief cavalry rides at the works in the plain; the rest of the relief army makes a demonstration in front of the Roman camp. Vercingetorix sees it from the citadel and brings his army out with the hooks and sheds he has been building. They engage on every side at once and go for whatever looks weakest. The Roman army is spread along its whole eleven miles and can barely meet them anywhere, and what most unnerves the men on the works is the shouting behind their backs, where their safety is in somebody else's hands.
phases.notes:
Time: Caesar's own. 'When noon now seemed to draw nigh' (VII.83) is the third and last stated time.

Day: this is the earliest reading of the day. Caesar's council, the choosing and the march run straight on from the dawn repulse, so the great assault falls on day 4. Ramsey and Raaflaub allow perhaps two days later and Livius has an uneventful day between. Napoleon III runs it as here.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

This is the phase the library's thumbnail and the battle page's card are drawn from. It is the only instant at which all three attacks and all four Roman sectors are in action at once, which is the picture of Alesia.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIII, closing sentence
references.quote: When noon now seemed to draw nigh, he marched hastily against that camp which we have mentioned before; and, at the same time, the cavalry began to approach the fortifications in the plain, and the rest of the forces to make a demonstration in front of the camp.

references.locator: book VII, chapter 83, section 8, the time word
references.quote: Cum iam meridies appropinquare videretur

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIV, Vercingetorix comes out
references.quote: Vercingetorix, having beheld his countrymen from the citadel of Alesia, issues forth from the town

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIV, the lines stretched thin
references.quote: The army of the Romans is distributed along their extensive lines, and with difficulty meets the enemy in every quarter.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIV, the shouting behind
references.quote: The shouts which were raised by the combatants in their rear, had a great tendency to intimidate our men, because they perceived that their danger rested on the valour of others

phases.label: Labienus goes to the north camp; Vercingetorix turns to the steep ground
phases.caption: At the upper lines the ground itself is against the defence: a little rise and a slope below it decide the fight. The Gauls come on in a testudo, fresh men relieving tired ones, and the earth they heap against the works both gives them a way up and buries the traps sunk in front. Caesar's men have no arms or strength left. He sends Labienus with six cohorts off Bussy to hold it, with leave to break out if he cannot. Inside the ring Vercingetorix gives up the works in the plain as too strong and attacks the steep ground under Flavigny instead, filling the ditches, clearing the way and pulling down the rampart with hooks; Brutus goes to that point with six cohorts, then Fabius with seven more.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. Caesar gives no time between noon and the end of the day, so this is a reading of the sequence of VII.85-86.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

Strength: the north camp keeps its full strength although Caesar says its men have no arms or strength left. Strength counts the fraction still fighting as part of the unit, not exhaustion, and exhaustion has nowhere to go but the caption. That is the one place here where the picture understates the words.

Heading: the Flavigny sector turns from its outer face at 180 to its inner one at 0, an exact half-turn and the second of the two. A sector fought from both sides at once takes the side the phase's caption is about, and this caption is about Vercingetorix on the steep ground below it. The turn resolves clockwise, through the east. The cohort counts, six, six, seven, and the four and forty of the next phase, are the battle's arithmetic and are drawn as arrows without numbers.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXV, the upper lines
references.quote: The principal struggle is at the upper lines, to which, we have said, Vergasillaunus was sent. The least elevation of ground, added to a declivity, exercises a momentous influence.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXV, the heaped earth
references.quote: The earth, heaped up by all against the fortifications, gives the means of ascent to the Gauls, and covers those works which the Romans had concealed in the ground. Our men have no longer arms or strength.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVI, Labienus sent
references.quote: Caesar, on observing these movements, sends Labienus with six cohorts to relieve his distressed soldiers

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVI, the attack on the steep ground
references.quote: The Gauls within, despairing of forcing the fortifications in the plains on account of the greatness of the works, attempt the places precipitous in ascent

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVII, Brutus and Fabius
references.quote: Caesar sends at first young Brutus, with six cohorts, and afterwards Caius Fabius, his lieutenant, with seven others

phases.label: Caesar's cloak: four cohorts and the horse strike the rear
phases.caption: The sally under Flavigny is beaten back, and Caesar rides for the quarter he sent Labienus to. He takes four cohorts out of the nearest redoubt on the way, orders part of the cavalry to follow him and part to ride right round the outside of the works and come at the Gauls from behind. Labienus, with neither rampart nor ditch holding, has gathered forty cohorts off the nearest posts and sends word of what he means to do. The men on the lines know Caesar is coming by the colour of his cloak. The legions drop their javelins and go in with the sword; the cavalry appears in the Gauls' rear; the sixty thousand turn their backs, and the killing begins.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate, from the sequence of VII.87-88.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

Heading: Vercassivellaunus's men are still faced at the camp they are storming when they break, so the heading holds at 135 and the flight is the caption's. The forty cohorts are quoted from Edwards because McDevitte drops the number the Latin carries; some editions read thirty-nine, which Napoleon III follows.

Strength: 40%, a reading of a body that is broken and ridden down but not yet destroyed.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVII, the four cohorts and the ride round
references.quote: drafts four cohorts from the nearest redoubt, and orders part of the cavalry to follow him, and part to make the circuit of the external fortifications and attack the enemy in the rear

references.locator: book VII, chapter 87, the forty cohorts
references.note: Quoted from Edwards because McDevitte drops the number the Latin carries, and read in the Internet Archive's OCR of the scan, whose line-break hyphens are closed up here.
references.quote: Labienus, finding that neither ramps nor trenches could resist the rush of the enemy, collected together forty cohorts, which had been withdrawn from the nearest posts and by chance presented themselves

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVIII, the colour of the robe
references.quote: His arrival being known from the colour of his robe

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVIII, the charge
references.quote: Our troops, laying aside their javelins, carry on the engagement with their swords. The cavalry is suddenly seen in the rear of the Gauls: the other cohorts advance rapidly; the enemy turn their backs; the cavalry intercept them in their flight, and a great slaughter ensues.

phases.label: Sunset: the relief flies; the besieged go back into the town
phases.caption: Sedulius of the Lemovices is killed, Vercassivellaunus is taken alive in the flight, seventy-four standards are carried to Caesar, and few of the sixty thousand get back to camp. The besieged watch the slaughter from the town and lead their men back off the works. The relief army breaks camp and runs the moment the news reaches it; only the state of the legions, worn out by reinforcing all day, saves any of it. After midnight the cavalry goes out after the rear, takes or kills a great many, and the rest scatter to their own states.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. 'the labour of the entire day' (VII.88) puts this at the end of the afternoon, and sunset falls about 18:00, computed rather than sourced. This phase also holds the midnight pursuit, which Caesar dates 'Immediately after midnight' and which the clock reaches inside this picture. A thirteenth phase for it would change only an arrow, so there is none.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1.

Strengths: the relief foot and horse at 50% and the sixty thousand at 10% are readings of 'few out of so great a number return safe to their camp' and of a flight overtaken in the dark. No source counts either.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVIII, the standards and the few who returned
references.quote: Sedulius the general and chief of the Lemovices is slain; Vergasillaunus, the Arvernian, is taken alive in the flight, seventy-four military standards are brought to Caesar, and few out of so great a number return safe to their camp.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVIII, the besieged withdraw
references.quote: The besieged, beholding from the town the slaughter and flight of their countrymen, despairing of safety, lead back their troops from the fortifications.

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXVIII, the wearied soldiers
references.quote: had not the soldiers been wearied by sending frequent reinforcements, and the labour of the entire day, all the enemy's forces could have been destroyed

references.locator: book VII, chapter LXXXIX, the midnight pursuit (in LXXXVIII in this edition)
references.note: This edition prints no heading for chapter LXXXIX: the pursuit, the surrender and the distribution of captives all sit under LXXXVIII, so every locator into 89 says where the passage stands here.
references.quote: Immediately after midnight, the cavalry are sent out and overtake the rear, a great number are taken or cut to pieces, the rest by flight escape in different directions to their respective states.

phases.label: Vercingetorix is delivered up before the camp
phases.caption: The next day Vercingetorix calls a council and tells them he took up the war for the general freedom and not for himself, and offers his own person either way: they may kill him to satisfy the Romans or hand him over alive. Envoys go to Caesar. He orders the arms surrendered and the chiefs brought out, seats himself at the head of the lines in front of the camp, and the Gallic chieftains are led before him. They give up Vercingetorix and lay down their arms. Plutarch has him ride out in his best armour, circle Caesar and sit down at his feet; Dio has him fall on his knees. Every man in the army but the Aedui and Arverni gets a captive.
phases.notes:
Time: an estimate. Caesar has only 'the following day' (VII.89). A council, an embassy and a surrender fill a morning, and the end at 15:00 is a guess.

Positions: Napoleon III's siting throughout, georeferenced as in phase 1. No source says which camp Caesar sat before; the plain below the town is the reading here, and it fits Plutarch's ride out through the gate.

The surrender scene is the one place where the three narratives differ openly, and all three are quoted.

Strengths: the besieged go to 0% with their arms laid down. The relief army's figures carry forward from the rout unchanged, because nothing counts what escaped.

references.quote: That he had undertaken that war, not on account of his own exigencies, but on account of the general freedom; and since he must yield to fortune, he offered himself to them for either purpose, whether they should wish to atone to the Romans by his death, or surrender him alive.

references.locator: Caesar 27, section 5
references.quote: He made a circuit round Caesar, who remained seated, and then leaped down from his horse, stripped off his suit of armour, and seating himself at Caesar's feet remained motionless, until he was delivered up to be kept in custody for the triumph.

references.locator: book XL, chapter 41, sections 1-2
references.quote: When quiet had been restored, he uttered not a word, but fell upon his knees, with hands clasped in an attitude of supplication.
